extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, photo editors and journalists (particularly in news organisations and the Arab region)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for photojournalists and editors on ethical standards, permissible image processing, and methods to verify and avoid manipulated images (including handling user-generated content). Emphasises credibility, legal/organizational codes, and practical detection tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider image manipulation as routine part of journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should always consider image manipulation; knowledge of manipulation techniques and how to spot them should be part of every journalist's skill set in order to tell news independently and factually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains increased risk due to proliferation of photography and social media; motivates why journalists must be aware of manipulation techniques and vigilant when selecting and publishing images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand photojournalism as a medium and its mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Photojournalists must understand photojournalism's concept and its role in improving credibility and conveying news truthfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing the history, culture and ethics of photojournalism helps avoid bad practices that mislead the public and undermines professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of legal, institutional and ethical frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must know the laws, covenants and professional codes governing media work (agency rules, national/international statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References and follow agency-specific guides (Reuters 'A Brief Guide to Standards, Photoshop and Captions', AP Code of Ethics for Photojournalists, NPPA Code of Ethics). These provide concrete rules on captions, camera settings and acceptable editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bias in image selection and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and editors must avoid letting personal, social, political or national loyalties influence image selection or editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bias can lead to publishing manipulated or misleading images; organisations must guard against choosing images that reinforce partisanship rather than accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-manipulation principle (do not change content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-manipulation means the image is presented in its complete form; the photographer must not change the content or delete/remove any part of the original photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit prohibitions: do not remove or add elements, do not copy/paste elements within the same image to alter content, do not add external parts from other images. Examples include AP/Reuters cases where adding or removing elements led to severed contracts and removal from archives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not add or remove people or objects (no fabrication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding elements to a photograph or removing elements (people, objects, defects) to change meaning is entirely unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies: Reuters Lebanon 2006 (added smoke), AP Syria 2013 (removed a video camera). Agencies required deletion from archives and disciplinary action. 'Adding elements to a photograph is entirely unacceptable and is in clear violation of AP's standards.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not stage, direct, or reenact events for news images
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers must not move elements, instruct subjects, reenact scenes or otherwise intervene to create or alter events before taking the photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging undermines reality of the image. Example: controversy around a photographer directing a child at a Brussels memorial; even posting on personal social media can harm professional credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption accuracy and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions must be clear and honest about who, what, why, when and how; any evasion of truth in accompanying description is a form of manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions should disclose relevant contextual information (including if the image is an enlargement, edited, or was taken earlier) and explain any necessary details so as not to mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate dating and provenance (do not misrepresent timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers and editors must not publish, send or broadcast an image taken on a prior date as if taken on a different date; editors must refer to the real date and reasons for delayed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misdating is considered misleading. If a photograph is used later, explicitly state the original date and why it was not published at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification procedure for eyewitness / UGC images
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with user-generated or eyewitness images, journalists should verify identity and provenance by asking: Who are they? Where are they? When did they get there? What can they see? Why are they there?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also request more photos from the same series, ensure the eyewitness is safe if in a dangerous location, and never avoid these basic verification questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical tools to check metadata and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ tools to extract metadata and detect editing: Jeffrey’s Exif Viewer, FotoForensics (ELA), Google Reverse Image Search, TinEye, JPEGSnoop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeffrey’s Exif Viewer reveals EXIF data (date/time, camera settings, sometimes GPS). FotoForensics uses error level analysis to highlight possible alterations. Reverse image searches help find original sources and earlier uses; JPEGSnoop analyses technical traces of edits. These tools aid provenance checks but are not infallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible image processing (limited, non-content-changing edits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissible steps generally include global lightening/shading (not selective dodging/burning that alters features), cropping for composition, color balance correction without changing composition, dust removal (sensor cleanup), resizing, and stating when an image is enlarged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change image content, do not copy elements within or from other images, and avoid processing that changes the meaning or features of the scene. If Photoshop or similar was used, provide a detailed explanation or caption as required by the organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose specific manipulations (enlargements, crops, edits)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an image is enlarged, partially used, or significantly edited, this must be stated (for example, mark 'enlargement').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Photoshop, write a detailed explanation in the caption or metadata so the photographer/editor avoids misrepresenting the image's provenance or intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain video integrity (do not alter audio/context to mislead)
rubrics_metrics.description: When editing video, maintain the soundness of content and general context; refrain from processing audio or other edits that may mislead viewers or distort the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any processing must not create a false impression; agencies' standards extend to video as well as still images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat subjects with respect and dignity; special care for victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers must treat all subjects with respect and dignity and give special consideration to subjects exposed to hardship (victims of crime/disaster), refraining from intrusive interference unless justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid photographing private moments of grief without clear justification; be mindful of the human impact of images and the ethics of representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pay or offer gifts to sources or photographed subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not provide financial awards, gifts, tips or compensation to sources or subjects for access or to influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes payments to intermediaries who arrange subjects. Payments that influence coverage undermine credibility and are prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sabotage other journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not sabotage the efforts of other journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional conduct includes cooperation and respect among journalists; undermining peers damages public trust in the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject, retract and remediate when manipulation is discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: If manipulation is discovered, news organisations must remove manipulated images from archives, notify clients/subscribers to delete them, and take appropriate disciplinary actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Reuters removed 920 images and cancelled a photographer's contract; AP severed ties with a photographer who removed a camera from an image. Agencies also issue subscriber advisories to delete manipulated images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional monitoring and oversight of press images
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for sufficient monitoring by international institutions and bodies to protect press images and detect digital falsification that may go undiscovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because digital manipulation is easy and can be sophisticated, organisations should invest in monitoring, standards, and training to preserve credibility; professional associations (e.g., NPPA) provide codes and training resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image accuracy and comprehensiveness as a core duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The image must be accurate and comprehensive in conveying the subjects; photo editors must not manipulate images and must ensure completeness of registration of subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid moulding with individuals or groups; remove personal or work biases; images should document society and preserve history without distortion.
